newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian PM rules out government reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Belgian PM rules out government reshuffle.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, working hard to keep his government in one piece, said on Monday he had no plans to alter it despite a scandal involving one of the parties in the coalition.
"There is not a single reason to reshuffle the government," Dehaene told reporters after a meeting of leaders of his own Flemish Christian Democratic party (CVP).

A scandal over bribes allegedly paid to the Francophone Socialist Party (PS) in the late 1980s has pressured Dehaene's government in recent weeks and provoked calls for the PS to leave the government and for the coalition to quit altogether.

Last week two former senior PS officials were charged with corruption in connection with an investigation into a 1989 bribes-for-airforce-contracts affair implicating French defence firm Dassault Aviation.
Their lawyers said that on behalf of the PS the officials, both aides to senior party politicians, received 30 million francs (about $1 million) from Dassault.
A former Belgian army colonel, reportedly a lobbyist for Dassault, has also been charged with corruption.

"This government has a clear mission and those who think I will let myself get distracted from this mission are wrong. This country currently needs a government that wants to meet its targets (and does not need) political games or a moment of vacuum," Dehaene said.
"I think that at this moment more than ever continuity is essential," he said.

Dehaene is eager to complete preparations for Belgium to join Europe's economic and monetary union, due to start in 1999, without major political difficulties which could bring down the government, whose term runs until 1999.
A group of young CVP politicians have urged the government to draw up a new government political accord, if necessary with new partners.

"We urgently need a big overhaul of the government... and to have a debate between the majority coalition partners on where it should go from here in the next two years to 1999," CVP member of parliament Luc Willems told BRTN radio.
But CVP chairman Marc Van Peel expressed the party's support for Dehaene after the party leaders' meeting.
"We are very clear on this...it is with this team that we want to complete the ride to 1999," he said earlier.
He also noted that there was growing pressure within the PS on politicians named in the Dassault affair to quit.
"It is important that we see within the PS...more and more votes are in favour of those responsible for a major corruption case to draw their conclusions," he said.
Leading PS politicians have urged Walloon regional parliament president Guy Spitaels to step down.
Legal moves to start questioning Spitaels, who was chairman of the PS at the time the Dassault bribes are alleged to have been paid, are under way.
The parliament is expected later on Monday to decide to lift his parliamentary immunity to allow the country's highest court to question him.
